title: Bias–Variance Trade-off
interviewAnswer: High bias means the model is too constrained and underfits; high variance means it fits training data but changes too much with the sample and generalizes poorly. Model complexity, regularization and data size shift this balance.
why: It connects model complexity, data size, regularization and generalization—so it is a compact test of ML maturity.
intuition: High bias: both train and validation performance are poor. High variance: training is strong but validation is much worse.
deepDive: Bias reflects systematic error from restrictive assumptions; variance reflects sensitivity to the sampled training set. More complex models typically reduce bias but can increase variance. Regularization, augmentation and more representative data often reduce variance.
math: Expected test error can be decomposed conceptually into bias² + variance + irreducible noise (under squared-error assumptions).
code:
# Practical diagnostic: compare train and validation curves
# High train error + high validation error -> likely high bias
# Low train error + much higher validation error -> likely high variance
commonMistakes: Saying “we want both bias and variance to be zero.” Irreducible noise and finite data prevent this ideal.
Calling every train/validation gap “overfitting” without checking split quality or leakage.
followUps: How does regularization affect bias and variance?
What do learning curves tell you?
Would more data help high bias or high variance more?
production: Diagnose with train/validation curves and slices before changing architecture. Sometimes the “variance problem” is actually a bad split or domain shift.
workedExample: A very shallow tree can underfit (high bias); an unrestricted tree can memorize training data (high variance); depth/regularization balances the two.

visual.title: Bias–variance trade-off
visual.caption: As model complexity grows, training error usually falls while validation error can eventually rise.
